lines.text: Do you know how rainbows work? Every rainbow is made by millions of tiny raindrops, each acting like a prism.
Sunlight looks white, but it's really every colour mixed together.
When light enters a raindrop, it slows down and bends. And each colour bends by a slightly different amount, so the colours fan apart.
The light bounces off the back of the drop, and bends again on the way out. It leaves at about forty two degrees for red, and forty for violet.
So you only see a rainbow with the Sun behind you. Every drop at that angle from your shadow sends you one colour, and together they form an arc.
From a plane, you can sometimes see the whole thing. A rainbow is really a full circle.
Light can bounce twice inside a drop, making a fainter second rainbow outside the first, with its colours flipped.
And the drops that make your rainbow aren't the ones making the rainbow of the person next to you. Everyone sees their own.
So a rainbow isn't a thing in the sky. It's an angle.
